Close To Hilbert

CurvesAlgorithmsLimits
Game: Watch a single curve grow into a path that winds all through a square.
How to play: Press Next step or click the picture to grow it. Switch between semicircles and tents, drag the slider, or press Reset to start over.
Look for the math

The applet replaces each straight piece of a curve by four smaller pieces. It starts with just one arc, yet after a few clicks the picture is a tight path through a square. The same trick works whether the little pieces are semicircles or tents.

Four copies of the previous step

Write the four directions as 0 down, 1 right, 2 up and 3 left. Step 1 is the word 1. Each later word is made as reverse3(previous) + previous + previous + complement(previous): the two middle copies are exactly the same, one outer copy is turned and reflected, and the other is complemented. That is an L-system rule, and it makes the word 4^(n-1) letters long at step n. The core was checked against the applet's own word over steps 1 to 10.

Smaller steps, same square

Every click halves the walking step, so four times as many pieces fit into the same region. The route's bounding rectangle is side wide and side - step high; as the step shrinks, those two lengths approach the same square. The curve is continuous: each new arc or tent starts where the last one ended. A check over steps 1 to 7 found that every crossing point of that grid lies within one shrinking step of the route, so in the limit the drawing gets dense in the square. This is what the page means by a space-filling curve. The finite pictures are not quite square, and an odd step makes the applet truncate its arc boxes by half a unit; both quirks are kept.

Close to Hilbert, not Hilbert

The classic Hilbert curve starts from a U shape and passes through every point of its grid once. Here the starting piece is one semicircle or one tent, so from step 3 onwards the route crosses some grid points twice. The page's claim about filling a square is therefore a claim about the limit, not about any one approximation: the test confirms the four-copy rule, the continuity and the shrinking grid, and also confirms those repeated crossings. Bogomolny notes that Hilbert himself gave his curve as one example of a general 1891 construction, which is what this applet illustrates.

Try switching between semicircles and tents at the deepest step: the route is identical, only the little bulges change.
